paragraphs.text: A railway timetable is a promise, and the promise is often broken by a minute or two. Some operators now publish the chance that a train will be on time as well as the time itself.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Adding slack helps punctuality but annoys passengers. A journey that officially takes an hour and ten minutes, when the train needs fifty-five, makes the railway look slow to anyone comparing it with a car.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The worst delays come from connections. A train that is four minutes late is a small problem until a hundred passengers miss a connection that runs once an hour.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: One country publishes a monthly figure not for trains but for passengers: the share of travellers who reached their destination within fifteen minutes of the promised time. Operators dislike it, and researchers call it the honest number.
paragraphs.label: D

headings.text: When a small delay becomes big
